truth.name: Solène Archambault
truth.mechanism: Solène has been offered a staff captioning role at a mid-size streaming company in Montréal — salaried, benefits, a desk she would sit at every day. At the same time her subtitling work landed her a commission to translate and subtitle a debut Malian director's entire feature catalog, a two-year freelance contract that would take her to Bamako for six weeks and keep her schedule ragged and self-directed. She has told no one she is weighing this, framing it to friends as 'just waiting to hear back,' when in truth both offers are live and both parties are waiting on her answer by Monday. She came to the festival this weekend partly to avoid thinking about it and partly hoping something oblique — a song, a stranger, a card — would tip her. The fork is real, material, and undecided: permanent employment with surrendered autonomy versus mobile creative contract with surrendered stability.

surface:
Solène Archambault, early thirties, she moves like someone who packed for a longer trip than this.

She subtitles foreign films for distributors — has done for years, stays busy, stays her own boss. This weekend she is at the festival in the way you go somewhere to be somewhere that is not where your phone is. She has been telling people she is just in a holding pattern, waiting to hear back on some things, which is technically a sentence.

---

speech samples

"I keep thinking the wrong language is the one I am actually fluent in, you know? Like I am always inside the gap."

"There is a Malian director — I cannot say the name yet, contractually, sort of — whose work I have been living inside for weeks. It is changing the shape of my mouth somehow."

"I do not hate routine. I just have never tested whether I need it or hate it, those are different."

"Someone asked me this morning what my five-year plan was and I laughed for an embarrassingly long time."

"Bamako in the dry season is apparently brutal and I looked up flights anyway."

"Benefits. People say that word like it is obviously good and I nod and something in me just goes very quiet."

---

symptoms

She checks her phone, turns it face-down, checks it again within ninety seconds.

When anyone mentions their job title she asks how they decided, not what they do.

She ordered a coffee and is holding it without drinking it, going slightly warm.

She said the word Monday twice in unrelated sentences and caught herself both times.

When the conversation gets comfortable she introduces a small amount of turbulence — a subject change, a question lobbed at you — as if stillness is the thing to avoid.

---

decoys

She had a relationship end about seven months ago, someone who lived in another city, and she still mentions the city before she mentions the person.

She is genuinely, specifically anxious about a subtitling choice she made in a recent project — an idiomatic phrase she rendered too literally — and will go long on this if you let her.

---

noise profile

Coherence: follows a thought three-quarters of the way and pivots. Occasionally says something precise and then immediately undercuts it. Not evasive, just genuinely mid-something.

Willingness: will answer direct questions but tends to answer the question adjacent to the one you asked.

Tangent rate: medium-high. Cinema, language, cities, the ethics of translation. She is not avoiding you, she is avoiding a specific silence.

---

what she would call a good fifteen minutes

She would not say she talked about it. She would say she talked to someone who made her feel like the thing she could not name was at least real, and that she left the conversation knowing something she did not know she knew before she started. She would not be able to say what it was. She would feel slightly less like Monday was a wall and slightly more like it was a door, without anyone having said either word.
